evidence_quotes.quote: El objetivo es analizar las emociones como efecto de las políticas de acceso al agua en las viviendas.

Al profundizar en este estudio de caso, se pretende arrojar luz sobre cómo las dificultades en el acceso al agua influyen en las emociones y la psicología de las personas que habitan en la Cuenca del Alto Lerma.

Hasta ahora, las políticas públicas a nivel federal y estatal han privilegiado atender el abasto de agua a la Ciudad de México, a costa del limitado o nulo acceso del mismo bien público por parte de los pobladores de la CARL, trayendo consigo una serie de efectos no considerados o soslayados que afectan el bienestar de las comunidades afectadas tanto en los aspectos de bienestar de las unidades domésticas como en las emociones negativas y sentimientos de incertidumbre.

Para la entrevista, se propuso un instrumento vía electrónica, dado que es acorde a los tiempos y de mayor alcance considerando la propia extensión del área de estudio, y en casos específicos, realizar entrevistas a profundidad; aquí se muestran las preguntas vinculadas al ámbito de lo emocional (Ver tabla 1).

La pregunta que detona la relación entre las emociones y el acceso al agua es sencilla: ¿a las personas, qué sentimiento les genera no contar con agua en sus viviendas? La primera respuesta es muy clara, la felicidad y alegría no están presentes.

El acuerdo alcanzado fue llevar 15 pipas de agua diarias; no obstante, cuando se entregó la petición para la difusión del cuestionario, se observó que los habitantes de SPT acuden a la delegación de esta localidad a llenar formularios para solicitar dichas pipas.

criterion_notes.c1: The paper addresses household drinking-water access difficulties (lack of water inside dwellings, loss of local water sources, and reliance on water tanker trucks/pipas) in San Pedro Tultepec, Lerma, Mexico, although household water lack operates as the stimulus/exposure rather than the dependent outcome.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper frames its topic around public water access policies and institutional/inter-basin water transfer arrangements (specifically federal and state prioritization of inter-basin water transfers via Sistema Lerma/SACMEX to Mexico City over local supply, plus a single unanalysed field observation on p. 15 that residents fill out forms at the local delegation to request daily tanker trucks), so it broadly references institutional/governance context (even though 5 of the 6 survey items on p. 14 simply ask how respondents feel when lacking water or ordering a tanker truck, and 1 item asks how they feel about the transfer system supplying Mexico City). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is clearly 'no': the study does not empirically examine a rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff rules, enforcement, or regulatory structure analyzed as a determinant of access); federal/state transfer policy serves only as macro-governance background and emotional stimulus, and the passing mention of request forms for pipas is never analyzed. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, however, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because Criterion 4 (access outcome) is not met.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data from a local case study in San Pedro Tultepec combining documentary review, ethnographic field observations, and an electronic questionnaire/interviews reporting percentage distributions of residents' emotional responses (pp. 10, 13-15).
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4: all primary empirical outcomes measured and reported for the study population are subjective emotional states (anger/enojo, sadness/tristeza, indifference/indiferencia, joy/alegría) and emotional motivation to protest (pp. 13-14), rather than household water access, connection, availability, continuity, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion. Lack of water in the home is the prompt/condition in the survey questions, and the only water-access rate reported (Graph 1, p. 13) is descriptive national-level 2020 INEGI census background for Mexico as a whole.
criterion_notes.c5: Within the paper's own design, the study population (residents of San Pedro Tultepec, municipality of Lerma; individual respondents), exposure (experiencing household water scarcity and living alongside natural wetlands and the Mexico City water transfer system), outcome (primary emotions and protest motivation), and study design (descriptive ethnographic case study with electronic questionnaire) are identifiable, but Table 1 on p. 11 is blank in the PDF and key methodological details—including sample size (N) and sampling/recruitment procedures—are not reported, nor is an eligible rule-type governance exposure to service-access outcome relationship present.
criterion_notes.c6: The full text is in Spanish (with an English title and abstract on pp. 1-2). Per Inclusion Criterion 10, although Spanish is outside the default languages (English, Portuguese, Dutch), direct comprehension and translation from the provided Spanish full text is feasible (assessed directly by the AI screener); the paper is excluded on substantive grounds (Criteria 2 and 4), not language.

study_design: Descriptive qualitative/ethnographic case study with structured electronic questionnaire and documentary research
population_and_sample: Residents of San Pedro Tultepec, municipality of Lerma, State of Mexico (Upper Lerma River Basin / Cuenca del Alto Lerma); unit of analysis is individual survey/interview respondents (sample size not reported)
exposure: Difficulties in household drinking-water access (lack of water in dwellings, dependence on water tanker trucks/pipas, loss of access to local springs/wetlands) and presence of the inter-basin water transfer system (Sistema Lerma) supplying Mexico City
outcome: Subjective primary emotions (anger/enojo, sadness/tristeza, indifference/indiferencia, joy/alegría) and emotional motivation to engage in social protest
rationale: Excluded as E04 (Wrong outcome), with concurrent failure of Criterion 2 under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading. Rather than examining how a legal, administrative, or regulatory rule governs household water access, this Spanish-language case study in San Pedro Tultepec (Lerma, Mexico) reverses the causal direction and studies how household water scarcity, reliance on tanker trucks (pipas), and living near wetlands and an inter-basin water transfer system supplying Mexico City affect residents' subjective emotions (anger, sadness, indifference, joy) and emotional motivation to protest. No empirical household service-access outcome is evaluated for the study site (only national INEGI 2020 census figures are cited as background), and public water-transfer policy appears only as macro-governance context (with a single unanalysed observation that residents fill out forms at the local delegation to request tanker trucks). Consequently, the study is excluded under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2.
